title: Errors & exception handling
summary: Read tracebacks, catch exceptions with try/except, and write code that fails clearly instead of crashing silently.
objectives: Tell the difference between syntax errors and runtime exceptions
Read a Python traceback from the bottom up
Catch errors with try and except blocks
Catch specific exception types instead of everything
Use else and finally for cleanup and follow-up code
Raise your own exceptions to signal bad input
Decide when to handle an error and when to let it crash

quiz.q: Which statement starts a block that handles errors in Python?
quiz.why: Python uses try to mark code that might fail, with an except block to handle the error.

quiz.q: When reading a traceback, which line tells you what actually went wrong?
options: Any line with a file path
quiz.why: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the final line names the exception type and message.

quiz.q: Why is catching a specific exception better than a bare 'except:'?
quiz.answer: A bare except hides unexpected bugs and catches things you did not mean to, like KeyboardInterrupt; naming the type only handles what you expect.
quiz.why: Catching too broadly swallows real problems and makes debugging much harder.

options: Runs only if no error occurred
Runs only if an error occurred
Runs no matter what, error or not
quiz.why: finally always runs, making it ideal for cleanup like closing files or connections.

quiz.q: Which keyword do you use to trigger an exception yourself?
quiz.why: raise lets you signal an error, for example raise ValueError("age must be positive").

quiz.q: True or false — a syntax error can be caught with try/except.
quiz.why: False. Syntax errors stop the code from running at all, so try/except never gets a chance to run.

body_markdown:
## Two kinds of errors

Python has two broad kinds of errors. A **syntax error** means the code is not valid Python — a missing colon or a stray bracket — and the program will not even start. A **runtime exception** happens while the program is running: the syntax is fine, but something goes wrong, like dividing by zero or opening a file that does not exist.

You cannot catch a syntax error with `try`/`except` because the code never runs. You *can* catch exceptions, and that is what this lesson is about.

## Reading a traceback

When an exception is not handled, Python prints a **traceback** and stops. Read it from the **bottom up**: the last line names the exception type and message; the lines above show the path of calls that led there.

```python
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

divide(10, 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

The final line, `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`, tells you exactly what happened.

## try / except

Wrap risky code in a `try` block. If an exception happens, control jumps to the matching `except` block instead of crashing.

```python
try:
    age = int(input("Age: "))
    print(100 / age)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type a whole number.")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Age cannot be zero.")
```

Catch **specific** exception types. A bare `except:` swallows everything — including bugs you did not anticipate — and makes problems invisible.

## else and finally

An `else` block runs only if the `try` succeeded with no exception. A `finally` block runs **no matter what**, which is perfect for cleanup.

```python
try:
    f = open("data.txt")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("No such file.")
else:
    print(f.read())
    f.close()
finally:
    print("Done attempting to read.")
```

## Raising your own exceptions

Use `raise` to signal that something is wrong — for example, invalid input to your own function. This fails loudly and early, which is far better than returning a wrong answer.

```python
def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("age must be positive")
    return age
```

## When NOT to catch

Do not catch an error just to hide it. If you cannot sensibly recover, let the program crash with its clear traceback — a silent failure is worse than a loud one. Catch errors only where you can do something useful: retry, use a default, or show the user a helpful message.

## Your task

Take a script that asks the user for a number and make it robust: keep asking until they give valid input, using `try`/`except`.

slides.title: Errors & exception handling
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One. Today we tackle something every programmer deals with constantly: errors. Far from being failures, errors are messages from Python telling you what went wrong. By the end of this lesson you'll read tracebacks with confidence, catch exceptions cleanly, and write code that fails clearly instead of crashing in a confusing way.

slides.title: Two kinds of errors
bullets: Syntax errors: invalid code, won't even run.
Runtime exceptions: code runs, then something breaks.
You can only catch exceptions, not syntax errors.
slides.narration: Python has two broad kinds of errors. A syntax error means the code itself isn't valid, like a missing colon, and the program won't even start. A runtime exception happens while the program is running. The syntax is fine, but something goes wrong, like dividing by zero. You can catch exceptions, but not syntax errors, because syntax errors stop the code before it ever runs.

slides.title: Reading a traceback
bullets: Python prints a traceback then stops.
Read it from the bottom up.
The last line names the error and message.
slides.code:
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

divide(10, 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
slides.narration: When an exception isn't handled, Python prints a traceback and stops. The trick is to read it from the bottom up. The very last line tells you the exception type and the message, here a Zero Division Error. The lines above it show the trail of function calls that led to the problem. Don't be scared of tracebacks; they're your best clue.

slides.title: try / except
bullets: Put risky code inside try.
If it fails, except handles it.
No crash — the program keeps going.
slides.narration: Here's the core tool. You put risky code inside a try block. If an exception happens, control jumps straight to the except block instead of crashing. In this example, if the user enters zero, we catch the Zero Division Error and print a friendly message, and the program carries on running normally.

slides.title: Catch specific types
bullets: Name the exact exception you expect.
Avoid a bare except — it hides real bugs.
You can have several except blocks.
slides.narration: Always catch the specific exception you expect, like Value Error when text can't become a number. A bare except with nothing after it catches absolutely everything, including bugs you never anticipated, and makes them invisible. You can stack several except blocks to handle different problems in different ways. Be precise, and your future self will thank you.

slides.title: else and finally
bullets: else runs only if try succeeded.
finally runs no matter what.
finally is perfect for cleanup.
slides.narration: Two more useful blocks. An else block runs only when the try succeeded with no exception, keeping your success path tidy. A finally block runs no matter what happens, whether or not an error occurred. That makes finally the ideal place for cleanup, like closing a file or a database connection. It always runs, so it never gets skipped.

slides.title: Raising your own errors
bullets: Use raise to signal a problem.
Fail loudly and early.
Better than returning a wrong answer.
slides.narration: You can also trigger exceptions yourself with the raise keyword. When your own function gets bad input, raising an error fails loudly and early. That's far better than quietly returning a wrong answer that causes confusing bugs much later. Here, a negative age raises a Value Error with a clear message explaining exactly what's wrong.

slides.title: When NOT to catch
bullets: Don't catch just to hide an error.
If you can't recover, let it crash.
Catch only where you can do something useful.
slides.narration: An important judgment call: don't catch an error just to silence it. If you can't sensibly recover, let the program crash with its clear traceback. A silent failure is far worse than a loud one, because you won't know anything went wrong. Catch errors only where you can actually do something useful, like retrying, using a sensible default, or showing the user a helpful message.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Using a bare except that hides bugs.
Reading the traceback top-down by mistake.
Catching an error then doing nothing.
Confusing syntax errors with exceptions.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that catch nearly everyone. One: using a bare except that swallows every bug. Two: reading the traceback from the top instead of the bottom. Three: catching an error and then doing nothing, which hides the problem. And four: confusing syntax errors, which stop the code, with runtime exceptions, which you can actually handle. Watch for these four.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Syntax errors stop your code before it runs, while runtime exceptions can be caught and handled. Read tracebacks from the bottom up to find the real cause. Use try and except to handle errors, naming the specific types you expect. Finally always runs for cleanup, and raise lets you signal bad input yourself. Your task: take a script that asks for a number and make it keep asking until the input is valid. Great work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
